newsitem.title: USA: Kansas wheat loss to freeze may exceed 100 mln bu.
newsitem.headline: Kansas wheat loss to freeze may exceed 100 mln bu.

text.p: Last week's freeze may have sliced more than 100 million bushels from the Kansas wheat crop and severe losses in Oklahoma also were likely, said crop specialists in those states.
In Kansas alone, last week's freeze may have cut production 100 million to 150 million bushels.

"Those numbers for Kansas alone are not unrealistic," said Rollie Sears, a Kansas State University wheat breeder, who this week toured the damaged areas. "The damage in the southern third of the state is worse than I thought."
In 1996, Kansas harvested 255.2 million bushels, and south central and southwest districts produced nearly 83 million bushels of that total.

Wheat damage from last weekend's freeze was most severe in south central and southwest Kansas, while lesser damage was seen in the middle third of the state. Across northern Kansas the wheat may have been harmed but should survive, said Sears.
Prior to the freeze, Kansas wheat was developing well and some analysts expected a 400-million-bushel crop this year, which would be the largest since the 1993 harvest of 433 million.
"There is a high percentage of the heads that have been killed," Sears said of southwest Kansas wheat.
He also found a high percentage of the ice-damaged wheat stems that were cracked and deteriorating.
In Oklahoma, wheat in the northwest section was hardest hit and some crop experts said 50 percent of the heads were lost.
"Most of the leaves and stems were burned back to the ground," said Mark Hodges, executive director of the Oklahoma Wheat Commission, of the northwest Oklahoma crop.
Prior to the freeze, some grain dealers expected an Oklahoma crop of 182 million bushels, nearly double last year's 93.10 milion harvest.
"We are now hoping for a 109 million (bushel) crop," said Butch Meibergen, president of W.B. Johnston Grain Co of Enid, Okla.
In the hardest-hit areas, Meibergen said it is unlikely the wheat will even produce secondary tillers. "Our immature tillers are dead and lying on the ground," he said.
Oklahoma's Farm Service Agency staff surveyed damaged fields this week and were expected to have a state-wide damage estimate next week, said an agency spokeswoman.
The freeze extended deep into the Texas Panhandle and across north Texas near Wichita Falls. However, due to the lack of physical damage, crop experts said it was difficult to estimate losses.
Todd Baughman, an extension agronomist near Wichita Falls, said the freeze may have sterilized the wheat heads, but that will not be known until the plants begin pollinating.
"I think we are going to have some damage, I just don't know how much," he said.
In 1996, Texas produced 75.4 million bushels of wheat.
